issues.legal_issue: A person for whose benefit property is expressly promised and who participated in and assented to the bargain may enforce that bargain by seeking specific performance.
material_facts: The written correspondence provided that the bungalow would be transferred into the claimant’s name and that she would bear the transfer expenses.

The evidence supported that the claimant demanded the bungalow and diamond ring and assented to the terms, even though communications could be made through her family because she was a purdah-observing woman.
The promisor delivered the ring to her, arranged for her to meet the sale-certificate stamp expenses, allowed her to occupy the bungalow, and permitted her to spend money on repairs and improvements.
The claimant remained in possession, and only execution of a conveyance remained outstanding.
issues.conclusion: The claimant was a party to the agreement as its promisee in respect of the bungalow and was entitled to demand its conveyance and seek specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: The court determined contractual participation from the terms of the correspondence, the evidence of the claimant’s demand and assent, and the parties’ conduct in performing the arrangement. A person who was the promisee under the agreement could enforce the promised conveyance. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement to transfer property.
predicates.agreement_identifies_claimant_as_transfe: The agreement provides that the property is to be transferred into the claimant’s name.
predicates.claimant_assented_to_property_bargain: The claimant demanded the property and assented to the terms of the bargain, directly or through communications made on the claimant’s behalf.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance suit concerns an agreement naming the claimant as transferee and the claimant assented to the property bargain, the claimant may enforce that bargain.

issues.legal_issue: A provision restricting suits concerning property purchased at an execution sale does not bar specific performance where the purchaser bought the property for itself and separately agreed to convey it to the claimant.
material_facts: The appellants purchased the bungalow in their own names at an auction sale in execution of a mortgage decree.
They had agreed that, after purchasing the bungalow, they would convey it to the claimant.
The court found that the appellants purchased the property for themselves so they could fulfil their agreement to convey it, and rejected the characterization of the purchase as benami.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not barred by section 66 of the Civil Procedure Code.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied section 66 of the Civil Procedure Code and held that it did not bar the suit in these circumstances: the appellants purchased the property for themselves, although they had agreed to convey it to the claimant. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement to transfer property.
predicates.purchaser_acquired_property_for_self: The purchaser acquired the property for the purchaser’s own account rather than as a benami holder for the claimant.
predicates.purchaser_agreed_to_convey_property_to_c: The purchaser agreed to convey the property to the claimant after acquiring it.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, where the purchaser acquired the property for itself and agreed to convey it to the claimant, the execution-sale bar does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: A substantial delay in seeking specific performance does not defeat the claim where the claimant has remained in possession and acted as owner, leaving only a formal document of title to be executed.
material_facts: The claimant had been in possession of the bungalow since soon after the agreement and continued to reside there.
She paid expenses relating to the property and spent substantial sums on repairs and improvements without objection from the appellants.
The claimant sought a conveyance, and the appellants refused to execute it; the remaining step was a formal document of title.
The argument that the passage of more than fourteen years and an altered position of the parties should defeat relief was raised on appeal.
issues.conclusion: The delay and asserted change in the parties’ position did not provide a ground to deny specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: Specific performance is discretionary, but the court held that delay and an asserted change in position did not defeat relief where the claimant had been in possession, borne property expenses, and made improvements, and only formal title remained to be conveyed. No provision or earlier case was relied on for this ruling.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and claimant_remained_in_possession and claimant_bore_property_expenses_and_made_improvements and only_formal_title_transfer_remained

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement to transfer property.
predicates.claimant_remained_in_possession: The claimant remained in possession of the property from shortly after the agreement through the time of suit.
predicates.claimant_bore_property_expenses_and_made: The claimant paid expenses relating to the property and spent money on repairs or improvements without objection.
predicates.only_formal_title_transfer_remained: The promised arrangement had otherwise been carried out, and execution of a formal title document remained outstanding.

issues.definition: When a claimant in a specific-performance suit remains in possession, bears property expenses and makes improvements, and only formal transfer of title remains, the claim is not defeated by delay.
